KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Due to high monthly astronomical tides, water levels will 
continue to be high during each high tide cycle thru the 
weekend. Based on storm surge forecasts, water levels will 
remain within action stage until Fri midday. It remains possible
that a small earlier timing difference in the arrival of 
strongest winds could lead to localized minor flooding during 
today and tonight's high tides as they are only within a half 
foot of flood stage already.

By midday Fri astronomical tides will be coming down but storm 
surge will be higher. Confidence would be slightly higher at 
water levels well into minor flood stage if winds were more 
onshore, but alongshore winds are likely and will still drive a 
storm surge towards the coast. Surge values roughly around 1 ft 
will bring us just over minor flood stage with waves building to
around 10 ft. Plus as you move southwest along the coast 
towards the Seacoast, winds will become more onshore. So a 
Coastal Flood Advisory has been issued given that this is not 
looking like a widespread moderate flooding kind of event. Aside
from the minor flooding Fri, beach erosion and overwash can be 
anticipated.

Guidance can also sometimes be too quick to lower storm surge 
behind a departing storm, especially if winds do not quickly 
turn offshore. So the Sat high tide will need to be monitored 
closely.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

High pressure remains overhead today, but will gradually slip 
east into the evening. Cirrus will thicken through the day, but 
temperatures should still rebound towards the 40s for highs. 

Rain associated with low pressure moving through the Mid- 
Atlantic and Ohio Valley arrives across southern NH late this 
afternoon. The primary band of precipitation will pass south to 
north across the forecast area overnight. 

Freezing Rain/Ice: CAD signal remains in place for the onset of
precipitation in the mountains and portions of the foothills 
later this evening. Precip will likely be in the form of 
freezing rain. The freezing rain is expected to fall on cold 
bare pavement. This will lead to the potential for glaze ice 
formation, generally less than a tenth of an inch, on untreated 
roads and surfaces, creating dangerous travel conditions 
tonight. NE winds will continue to strengthen as the evening 
goes on, providing reinforcing cold air at the surface from a 
radiating source region of eastern ME and New Brunswick. Should 
the coastal low form and deepen, cooler values will be possible 
into the interior with a sharp temperature gradient developing 
from coast to 20 or 25 miles inland. The Winter Weather Advisory
was expanded southward into the foothills in anticipation of 
the CAD holding strong through today. As the stacked low 
circulation approaches the area Friday midday, CAD begins to 
weaken with warmer air beginning to infiltrate NE.

Rain: Most of the rain falls in little more than a 6 hour 
period at any given location overnight. Portions of southern NH 
could see rates begin to taper after 1am, and before sunrise for
central/southern ME as drier air arrives aloft. REFS 3hr QPF is
quite robust (around 1.25" with 80% chance greater than 1 inch)
along the NH Seacoast up through the I95 corridor to 
Portland...likely latching on to a coastal front enhancement as 
the occlusion lifts. Ensemble guidance has been retreating from 
the idea, but this could be hires guidance attempting to resolve
a secondary low along the coast. All rain is expected for 
southern NH and coastal/interior ME with light rain or drizzle 
continuing through Friday morning.

Wind: The potent LLJ associated with the storm is expected to 
weaken as it lifts north into central and northern New England. 
This will keep winds gusty, but not strong enough for mention of
more widespread impacts. The gusty winds will blow around 
unsecured objects and break some tree limbs, leading to a 
limited power outage threat. The coast and ridges/western slopes
of the Monadnocks/Whites will see the brunt of winds this 
evening and overnight, slackening Friday morning. All of these 
locations are dependent on breaking a strong inversion in the 
low levels either by elevation (Whites/Monadnocks, inc 
downslope) or surface warm air advection off the Gulf of Maine 
(coast and southern NH). Wind fetch should be strong enough to 
overcome any weak CAD through the far southern ME coast into 
southern NH. This leaves the window open for gusts up to 40 mph 
this evening, continuing up the ME coast. Gust factor falls off 
quickly further inland due to the expected inversion, around 20 
mph.
